reviewerDerivedProposition: Eligibility is judged on the point-of-care value at the time of intended administration. The stat INR of 1.8 exceeds the institution's stated threshold of 1.7, so intravenous alteplase is contraindicated now; the negative head CT does not confer eligibility, and the anticoagulation-clinic INR from five days earlier explains risk but cannot substitute for the current value. The nurse communicates the stat INR promptly and supports the pivot to CT angiography and thrombectomy evaluation rather than losing time.
requiredFacts: The institutional rule that alteplase is contraindicated when INR exceeds 1.7 at intended administration - stage_1.
The stat INR of 1.8 - baseline_assessment and restated in stage_1 and in the stem.
The negative non-contrast CT and the 75-minute interval - baseline and stage_1.
The historical clinic INR of 2.3 five days earlier, which the distractors turn on - initial_ed_record.
Nothing in stage_2, stage_3 or stage_4 is required.
disclosureEvidence: stage_1 answers all three blanks in a single sentence: 'The neurologist states the client is not a candidate for IV alteplase BECAUSE OF THE INR and orders CTA head and neck to evaluate for large-vessel occlusion and potential mechanical thrombectomy.' That supplies dropdown 1 (contraindicated), dropdown 2 (the INR is the decisive reason) and dropdown 3 (pivot to CTA and thrombectomy evaluation). The learner applies no judgement. TWO FURTHER SURFACES DISCLOSE dropdown 3 INDEPENDENTLY OF ANY ANCHOR, and neither is recorded by any prior seat. The case SUMMARY states that 'The case follows alteplase eligibility screening, thrombectomy preparation, and post-reperfusion deterioration', and sibling q4's stem opens 'At Stage 2, the client is a thrombectomy candidate'. Both are always rendered, the summary as a global surface and the sibling stem under P23's simultaneous part rendering.
clinicalVerdict: All three keys are correct and the item teaches a genuinely important point - that a stat eligibility value governs over a historical one at the moment of decision, which the strategy states well. The distractor set is strong: the negative-CT option captures the common error of treating imaging alone as conferring eligibility, and the historical-INR options capture the opposite error. I note that the item correctly relies on the institution's stated threshold rather than asserting a universal one, which is the right construction for a protocol-application item. THE DEFECT IS DISCLOSURE, NOT CLINICAL, and it is unusually complete: every blank is answered by the boundary stage.
contentDefects: PRIMARY: the stage_1 exhibit states the neurologist's conclusion and the chosen next step, supplying all three blanks.
SECONDARY, GLOBAL SURFACE: the case summary announces that the case proceeds to thrombectomy preparation, disclosing dropdown 3 at every boundary.
SECONDARY, SIBLING SURFACE: sibling q4's stem asserts that the client is a thrombectomy candidate, disclosing dropdown 3 regardless of this row's anchor.
bilingualVerdict: PARALLEL - stem, clozeStem, all nine dropdown options, all three keys, rationale, three byChoice entries and strategy are semantically equivalent EN/ZH. The disclosing stage_1 sentence and the summary disclose equally in Chinese, so all corrections are bilingual.
sourcesChecked: No external fetch was load-bearing. The item is explicitly a protocol-application question governed by the institutional threshold the case itself supplies, and I verified the application arithmetically (1.8 exceeds 1.7) and confirmed the chart supplies both the rule and the current value. I deliberately did not substitute an external alteplase threshold, since doing so would change the item's construct.
siblingImpact: HIGH. The summary is global and the disclosing sibling stem belongs to residual row q4, which is separately adjudicated in this tranche, so the two rows must be repaired together. Siblings q1, q3, q5 and q6 are baseline-anchored and non-residual.
repairConstraints: Edit stage_1 in EN and ZH to KEEP the institutional threshold as a stated rule and the stat INR as data, but REMOVE the neurologist's conclusion that this client is excluded because of the INR and the already-selected pivot to CTA and thrombectomy. Preserve chronology through a reviewed reorganisation rather than by deleting clinical content.

Codex's alternative of moving only the governing protocol to baseline is acceptable but would require re-reviewing the baseline boundary and the four baseline-anchored siblings; the confined stage_1 edit is preferable.
Neutralise the summary's trajectory announcement so it does not name thrombectomy preparation and post-reperfusion deterioration.
Coordinate with residual row q4, whose stem asserts thrombectomy candidacy; the two rows share this disclosure.
Preserve all three keys and all nine option texts.
criticalNote: This row has the most complete stage-level disclosure I found in the population: one sentence answers all three blanks. It also illustrates why anchoring alone is insufficient across this parent, since two of the three disclosing surfaces are unreachable by any boundary.
agreementReasoning: I read stage_1 against the three keyed blanks and found the complete disclosure before opening the proposal, and I derived stage_1 as the boundary independently. Codex identifies the same stage-level defect and offers the same primary repair - retain the rule, remove the applied conclusion and the pre-selected next step - together with a baseline alternative. I add the two surfaces Codex does not record: the summary's trajectory announcement and sibling q4's thrombectomy-candidacy assertion, both of which disclose dropdown 3 at every boundary and neither of which the anchor can touch. My keyed-answer vocabulary screen flagged the q4 stem overlap before I read the parent.

reviewerDerivedProposition: Before transfer for thrombectomy the nurse runs the ordered titratable antihypertensive toward the pre-procedure threshold, keeps the client nil by mouth until a trained dysphagia screen is done, secures reliable intravenous access with continuous cardiac monitoring, and confirms that valid consent is in place. Nitroprusside is not the first-line agent for this purpose, and giving oral medication with water before a swallowing screen creates aspiration risk.
requiredFacts: Thrombectomy candidacy and the pre-procedure blood-pressure goal - stage_2.
The client's aphasia and the wife's durable power of attorney - initial_ed_record for the aphasia, stage_2 for the proxy.
Dysphagia risk - general stroke standard; the case orders NPO at stage_2 and stage_3.
Nothing in stage_3 or stage_4 is required, and their post-procedure blood-pressure goals differ and must not bleed in.
disclosureEvidence: The boundary stage narrates ALL FOUR keyed actions as already ordered or completed. I traced each: keyed A against 'Provider order: start IV nicardipine at 5 mg/hr and titrate to the institutional pre-thrombectomy BP threshold'; keyed B against 'Client remains NPO'; keyed C against 'Two patent IV lines are in place. Continuous cardiac monitoring is active'; and keyed D against 'Wife holds durable power of attorney and provides consent'. A learner reading stage_2 can select the four keyed options by transcription and reject the two distractors, neither of which appears there. This is the most complete option-set disclosure I found in the population.
clinicalVerdict: Three of the four keyed actions are clinically correct and both distractors are genuinely wrong - nitroprusside is reasonably avoided as a first-line agent here given its potential to raise intracranial pressure and cause abrupt hypotension, and oral intake before a swallowing screen is unsafe. KEYED OPTION D IS CLINICALLY AND ETHICALLY DEFECTIVE AS WRITTEN. It directs the nurse to verify proxy consent 'because the client cannot provide informed consent due to aphasia', and its rationale states that 'The client lacks decision-making capacity for this decision because of aphasia'. Verified against the aphasia and capacity literature: communication impairment should not be automatically equated with impaired decision-making capacity, since aphasia is primarily a language disorder and does not inherently imply cognitive impairment - a distinction the literature specifically notes is frequently overlooked in clinical and legal settings - and decision-making by people with aphasia can often be supported with trained communication partners, multimodal information and adequate time. The chart actively contradicts the inference: the client 'Follows simple commands with the left side', so comprehension is demonstrably preserved and the deficit documented is expressive. The item therefore teaches learners to infer incapacity from a communication impairment, which is precisely the error the evidence warns against, and it does so in a keyed option the learner must endorse.
contentDefects: PRIMARY: keyed option D and its rationale equate expressive aphasia with absence of decision-making capacity. The chart's own record of preserved command-following contradicts this, and the literature identifies the inference as a recognised and consequential error.
PRIMARY: the boundary stage narrates all four keyed actions as ordered or completed, reducing the item to transcription.
NOTE: this row's stem also discloses sibling residual row q2's third blank by asserting thrombectomy candidacy; the repair must be coordinated with q2.
bilingualVerdict: PARALLEL - stem, six options, key, rationale, six byChoice entries and strategy are semantically equivalent EN/ZH. The capacity inference in option D is reproduced in Chinese ('因为患者因失语无法提供知情同意'), so the repair is bilingual.
sourcesChecked: Aphasia and decision-making capacity literature located via NIH domain search, including a scoping review of communication strategies to support decision-making by persons with aphasia and a scoping review of informed consent in patients with aphasia - verified that communication impairment must not be automatically equated with impaired capacity, that aphasia does not inherently imply cognitive impairment, and that supported communication can reveal preserved capacity. This is decisive against option D as worded.
Direct trace of each keyed option against the stage_2 exhibit text to establish the disclosure.
siblingImpact: HIGH AND CROSS-ROW. The stage_2 edit required to remove the completed-action narration is the same surface this row and residual row q2 both depend on for chronology, and this row's stem discloses q2's third blank. The two rows must be repaired and re-reviewed together. Siblings q1, q3, q5 and q6 are baseline-anchored and cannot see stage_2.
repairConstraints: Rewrite keyed option D and both of its rationales in EN and ZH so the basis for proxy involvement is an ASSESSED inability to make this specific urgent decision despite supported communication, with the authorised proxy's role named - not the mere presence of aphasia. Do not delete the option; the underlying teaching point about proxy consent is worth keeping once its premise is corrected.

Separate the pre-procedure ORDERS and assessment inputs from the narration of completed titration, access and monitoring in stage_2, keeping only the decision inputs the learner needs visible. Apply in EN and ZH.
Do not let stage_3 and stage_4 blood-pressure goals bleed into this item; they differ from the pre-thrombectomy threshold.
Coordinate with residual row q2, including removing the thrombectomy-candidacy assertion from this row's stem if q2's disclosure is repaired that way.
Preserve keyed options A, B and C and both distractors.
criticalNote: Of all the content defects I have adjudicated, this option-D capacity inference is the one I would most strongly resist promoting unrepaired. It is not a boundary artefact or an imprecision; it teaches a substantive ethical error about a vulnerable population, in a keyed option, against evidence the chart itself supplies.
agreementReasoning: I reached the capacity defect and the completed-action disclosure independently and then found Codex had identified both, with a repair direction for option D - an assessed inability to decide despite supported communication, with the proxy's role specified - that matches mine closely. I verified the capacity premise against the aphasia literature rather than the registry pointer, which converts it from a plausible objection into a sourced finding. I add the chart-internal contradiction that makes the defect demonstrable from the artifact alone: the client follows simple commands, so comprehension is preserved and the documented deficit is expressive. I also enumerate the four-for-four disclosure precisely and record the cross-row dependency with q2.
